To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) O6-ethylG is a highly mutagenic base analog in E. coli, (2) O6-alkylG is repaired by the uvrB-dependent repair system of E.coli, and (3) the uvrABC repair system is more efficient at removing O6-alkG from a sequence that is adjacent to an A:T base pair than from a sequence not adjacent to an A base pair.

(1) the mutagenic specificity of EMS is similar in UvrB- and Uvr+ strains of E. coli; (2) the frequency of mutation is higher in the UVRB- strain than in the Uvr+ strains; (3) the frequency of induced mutation is dependent on neighboring base pair context; and (4) the UvrABC repair system of E.coli is effective at removing O6-ethyl guanine lesions from DNA.

(1) the UvrABC excision system of E. Coli repairs 6-ethylguanosine, (2) the UvrB protein is the component of the excision repair system that interacts with 6-ethyl- guanosine and, (3) 6-ethyl guanosine is repaired most efficiently if it is adjacent to an A:T base pair.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mutagenic specificity of ethylating agents in E. coli, and the effect of the excision repair system, uvrB, on mutagenesis.
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms involved in the repair of DNA damaged by alkylating agents.
the study of the mutagenic specificity of the alkylating agent, ethyl methanesufonate, at the molecular level.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the uvrABC repair system of E.coli is capable of removing the O6-ethyl guanine lesions from the DNA, but not with equal efficiency at all sites in the genome.
the uvrABC system in E. coli is able to repair the majority of O6-ethylated guanine bases, with the exception of those adjacent to A:T pairs.
EMS-induced mutagenicity and its site specificity are not significantly affected by UvrB protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
O6-ethylation of guanine in DNA is repaired by the uvr system of E. colli and the repair system acts preferentially on lesions adjacent to A: T base pairs.
the uvrABC system in E. coli repairs O6-ethyl guanine lesions in a sequence-specific manner, but that the sequence-specificity of the repair is not absolute.
EMS mutagenesis in UvrB- E. coli occurs predominantly at G:C base pairs, with a slight preference for those base pairs flanked by an A:T pair.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the uvrABC system can be very specific and efficient at repairing O6-ethyl-guanine.
the mutagenic spectrum of EMS in E. coli is very narrow, and that this mutagenic spectrum is not significantly influenced by the UvrB subunit of the excision repair system.
the UvrB protein is the key factor in the repair of the O6-ethyl-guanine lesions.
